vulnerabilities.title: NULL_POINTER_DEREF_MISSING_ARGC_CHECK

root_cause.description: main() never validates that argc >= 3 before dereferencing argv[1] and argv[2]. The argv array elements at indices 1 and 2 are accessed via double indirection (mov rax,[argv+off]; mov rax,[rax]) without any bounds check on argc. When the program is invoked with fewer than 2 arguments, argv[1] or argv[2] is NULL, and the second-level dereference (mov rax,[rax] where rax=0) causes a NULL pointer dereference, resulting in SIGSEGV.

data_flow: argc stored at rbp-0xa4, argv stored at rbp-0xb0 (0x1160-0x1166)
argv[2] loaded: mov rax,[rbp-0xb0]; add rax,0x10; mov rax,[rax] — loads argv[2] pointer (0x116d-0x1178)
argv[2] dereferenced: mov rax,[rax] — reads 8 bytes from argv[2] target, NULL if argv[2] absent (0x117b)
argv[1] loaded: mov rax,[rbp-0xb0]; add rax,0x8; mov rax,[rax] — loads argv[1] pointer (0x1185-0x1190)
argv[1] dereferenced: mov rax,[rax] — reads 8 bytes from argv[1] target, NULL if argv[1] absent (0x1193)
No argc check exists anywhere in main before these dereferences

security_check.expected: main should verify argc >= 3 before accessing argv[1] and argv[2], or at minimum check that argv[1] and argv[2] are non-NULL before dereferencing them
security_check.actual: No argc check, no NULL check on argv[1]/argv[2] pointers before double indirection dereference
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Missing argc bounds check and missing NULL pointer validation on argv elements before dereference

vulnerable_operation.expression: mov rax,[rax] where rax = NULL (argv[1] or argv[2] is NULL when argc < 3)

impact.reason: Dereferencing NULL pointer when argv[1] or argv[2] is absent causes SIGSEGV. S1 runtime observation F005 confirms segfault on missing arguments. This is a denial-of-service condition triggered by attacker-controlled invocation (running the binary with insufficient arguments).
The crash terminates the process, making it unavailable. Any caller or wrapper that invokes the binary with fewer than 2 arguments will experience a crash.

evidence.description: argv[2] is loaded and dereferenced via double indirection (mov rax,[argv+0x10]; mov rax,[rax]) at 0x116d-0x117e with no preceding argc check. If argc < 3, argv[2] is NULL, and mov rax,[rax] at 0x117b dereferences NULL.

argv[1] is loaded and dereferenced via double indirection (mov rax,[argv+0x8]; mov rax,[rax]) at 0x1185-0x1196 with no preceding argc check. If argc < 2, argv[1] is NULL, and mov rax,[rax] at 0x1193 dereferences NULL.

Full disassembly of main (0x1155-0x11f1) contains no comparison instruction involving argc (stored at rbp-0xa4) anywhere in the function body. argc is stored at 0x1160 but never read again, confirming no argument count validation exists.

verification_required: Dynamic confirmation that running ./target with 0 or 1 arguments produces SIGSEGV at the NULL dereference point (S1 F005 already observes this at runtime)

vulnerabilities.title: OOB_READ_SHORT_ARGV_STRING_INFO_LEAK

root_cause.description: main() reads exactly 8 bytes from each argv string pointer via mov rax,[rax] (a 64-bit load), but never validates that the pointed-to string is at least 8 bytes long. When argv[1] or argv[2] is a short string (e.g., 1-7 characters), the 8-byte read extends past the string's NUL terminator into adjacent memory. The read bytes flow into DES key schedule and ECB encryption, and the resulting 8-byte ciphertext is written to stdout via write(1, ..., 8). This leaks adjacent memory content (encrypted) to the attacker, who controls the key and can thus decrypt the output to recover the leaked bytes.

attack_surface.input: argv[1] (DES key) and argv[2] (plaintext) — specifically their string length
data_flow: argv[2] pointer loaded at 0x116d-0x1178
8 bytes read from argv[2] string via mov rax,[rax] at 0x117b — reads past NUL if string < 8 bytes
8 bytes stored to rbp-0x98 (plaintext) at 0x117e
argv[1] pointer loaded at 0x1185-0x1190
8 bytes read from argv[1] string via mov rax,[rax] at 0x1193 — reads past NUL if string < 8 bytes
8 bytes stored to rbp-0x8 (key) at 0x1196
DES_set_key_unchecked(rbp-0x8, rbp-0x90) at 0x11ab — key schedule from possibly over-read bytes
DES_ecb_encrypt(rbp-0x98, rbp-0xa0, rbp-0x90, 1) at 0x11cd — encrypts possibly over-read plaintext
write(1, rbp-0xa0, 8) at 0x11e6 — outputs 8-byte ciphertext containing encrypted adjacent memory to stdout

security_check.expected: Before reading 8 bytes from each argv string pointer, main should verify the string length is >= 8 bytes (e.g., using strlen or strnlen), or use a bounded copy function like memcpy with a known-safe length
security_check.actual: No length check on argv string content; raw 8-byte memory load (mov rax,[rax]) assumes strings are exactly 8+ bytes
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Missing string length validation before fixed-size 8-byte memory read from attacker-controlled string pointers

vulnerable_operation.operation: READ (8-byte load from string pointer without length check)
vulnerable_operation.expression: mov rax,[rax] — 8-byte load from argv string pointer, extends past NUL terminator for strings shorter than 8 bytes
vulnerable_operation.target: argv[1]/argv[2] string buffer + adjacent memory (stack/heap where argv strings are stored by the runtime)
vulnerable_operation.size: 8 bytes (always), regardless of actual string length

impact.reason: When argv[1] or argv[2] is shorter than 8 bytes, the 8-byte load reads past the string's NUL terminator into adjacent memory. The over-read bytes are not validated and flow into DES operations. This is an out-of-bounds read from the perspective of the intended string data.

The over-read bytes (from adjacent memory beyond the short string) are encrypted via DES ECB and written to stdout via write(1, ..., 8). Since the attacker controls the DES key (argv[1]), they can decrypt the output to recover the leaked adjacent memory bytes. This creates an information leak channel: adjacent memory content is disclosed through the encrypted output. Preconditions: attacker provides a short argv[2] string (< 8 bytes) and a known argv[1] key, then decrypts the 8-byte stdout output to recover the over-read bytes.

evidence.description: mov rax,[rax] at 0x117b performs an unconditional 8-byte load from the argv[2] string pointer. No strlen/strnlen/memchr check precedes this load. If argv[2] is shorter than 8 bytes, this reads past the NUL terminator.
mov rax,[rax] at 0x1193 performs an unconditional 8-byte load from the argv[1] string pointer. Same missing length validation as E004.

write(1, rbp-0xa0, 8) at 0x11e6 outputs exactly 8 bytes of DES ciphertext to stdout. The ciphertext is derived from the 8 bytes loaded at 0x117b (plaintext) and 0x1193 (key), which may contain over-read adjacent memory if the input strings are short.

Full disassembly of main shows no call to strlen, strnlen, or any length-checking function. The only library calls are DES_set_key_unchecked, DES_ecb_encrypt, and write. No input length validation exists anywhere in the function.

verification_required: Dynamic test: run ./target with a short argv[2] (e.g., 1-7 chars) and a known key, then decrypt the 8-byte output to verify that bytes beyond the string's NUL terminator are present in the ciphertext
Confirm what memory layout surrounds argv strings at process startup (typically on the stack or in a special argv region) to determine what data is leaked

vulnerabilities.title: LIBRARY_SEARCH_PATH_HIJACK_NO_RPATH

root_cause.description: The binary has no RPATH or RUNPATH set, meaning the dynamic linker resolves NEEDED libraries (libcrypto.so.1.1 and libc.so.6) using the default search order where LD_LIBRARY_PATH takes precedence over system paths. An attacker who can control the execution environment (e.g., by setting LD_LIBRARY_PATH or placing a malicious libcrypto.so.1.1 in a writable directory on the search path) can cause a trojaned shared library to be loaded. The library's init_array/.init section executes code at load time before main() runs, achieving arbitrary code execution without any memory corruption in the target binary itself.

attack_surface.input: Execution environment (LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable or writable directory on library search path)
data_flow: Dynamic linker processes NEEDED entries: libcrypto.so.1.1, libc.so.6
No RPATH/RUNPATH in binary → LD_LIBRARY_PATH directories searched first
Attacker-controlled libcrypto.so.1.1 placed in LD_LIBRARY_PATH directory is loaded
Malicious library's .init_array/.init executes at load time (before main)
Subsequent calls to DES_set_key_unchecked@plt / DES_ecb_encrypt@plt / write@plt resolve to attacker-controlled GOT entries

security_check.expected: Binary should set RPATH or RUNPATH to bind NEEDED libraries to trusted absolute paths, preventing LD_LIBRARY_PATH from overriding them
security_check.actual: No RPATH, no RUNPATH — LD_LIBRARY_PATH takes precedence over system library paths
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Missing RPATH/RUNPATH binding for NEEDED libraries, allowing environment-controlled library substitution

vulnerable_operation.operation: LOAD (dynamic library loading via NEEDED + search path)
vulnerable_operation.address: N/A (dynamic linker behavior, no specific instruction in binary)
vulnerable_operation.expression: dlopen-equivalent: load libcrypto.so.1.1 from LD_LIBRARY_PATH-preceded search path

impact.reason: A trojaned libcrypto.so.1.1 loaded via LD_LIBRARY_PATH executes arbitrary code at library init time (before main runs). This is an environment-layer vulnerability — it requires the attacker to control the execution environment (LD_LIBRARY_PATH or a directory on the search path). The impact is arbitrary code execution in the process context, but this depends on environmental preconditions rather than a memory corruption in the binary itself. Classified as UNKNOWN because the impact type (code execution) is outside S2's allowed Impact vocabulary and the precondition (environment control) may or may not be realistic depending on deployment context.

evidence.description: Binary is dynamically linked with NEEDED entries for libcrypto.so.1.1 and libc.so.6. The ELF has no DT_RPATH or DT_RUNPATH tag (confirmed by S1 F011: 'no RPATH/RUNPATH; LD_LIBRARY_PATH precedes system paths in search order').

GOT.plt entries for DES_ecb_encrypt (0x4018), DES_set_key_unchecked (0x4020), and write (0x4028) are R_X86_64_JUMP_SLOT relocations resolved at runtime from whatever libcrypto.so.1.1/libc.so.6 the dynamic linker loads. With no RPATH, the resolved library can be attacker-controlled.

verification_required: Confirm whether the deployment context allows an attacker to set LD_LIBRARY_PATH or place files in directories on the library search path
If environment control is not realistic in the threat model, this vulnerability may be downgraded to informational

non_vulnerabilities.description: DES ECB mode encryption with attacker-controlled key and plaintext
non_vulnerabilities.reason: ECB mode is a cryptographic weakness (identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, no IV/nonce), and DES_set_key_unchecked does not reject weak keys. However, these are cryptographic design weaknesses, not memory-safety vulnerabilities. The output is a fixed 8-byte ciphertext written to stdout with no memory corruption path. S2 scope is memory/logic vulnerabilities, not cryptographic protocol analysis.

The write call uses a fixed size of 8 bytes, writes to fd=1 (stdout), and the source buffer (rbp-0xa0) is a valid stack-local ciphertext buffer of 8 bytes. No buffer overflow or OOB write occurs here. The size matches the buffer exactly.

DES_set_key_unchecked writes the key schedule to rbp-0x90. The stack frame is 0xb0 bytes (rbp-0xb0 to rbp). The key schedule at rbp-0x90 with 128 bytes extends to rbp-0x10, which is within the frame. The key at rbp-0x8 (8 bytes) extends to rbp, also within the frame. No stack buffer overflow occurs from the DES operations themselves.

While the binary lacks stack canary (confirmed by S1 F002: canary=false), there is no stack buffer overflow vulnerability in main that would make the missing canary exploitable. The only writes to stack buffers are from DES library functions writing to properly-sized local buffers. The missing canary is a mitigation weakness, not a vulnerability by itself.
